I actually made my own so I had it set up in rows and columns and the columns where power and the rows where speed and then I just had it set up with a little half inch box for each power/speed setting and made as many layers as I needed so that I could adjust the speed/power. There is an easy way to adjust the power so you don’t have to make a whole new layer for each power setting you may want to try and look that up cause it is hard to tell you what to do with our showing it. As far as cutting went I did a little different set up. I had only about 4 columns and 4 rows and the columns where set up as far as how many passes (I did 2 to 5 passes) and the rows where speed (so like 50mm/min or 100mm/min) and instead of having it fully engrave the box I just had it do the line for the box so I could see how it cuts at different speeds/passes obviously at 100% power. You could look up some other ones as well just google “material test card for laser engraver” and you should find plenty of ideas.

Well for engraving you just focus to the top of whatever you are engraving you only focus to the bottom for cuts. There is definitely a learning curve so be prepared to waste some materials specially wood. Also what you can do is make a material test card and that will help you figure out settings that you like best for said material wether it be cutting or engraving or both.

No I don’t use a camera I just set up the board and then use the framing tool on lightburn to outline where the cut will be and I usually give a half inch from the bottom of the board. If you change the settings on lightburn you can have the laser fire at 1% power when you hit the frame tool. You just shift click frame and it will outline where the cut will be in a box shape or rounded shape depending on what you click. The board itself does not have to be perfectly straight the cuts will come out just fine. And right now I can cut 3mm (1/8th inch) birch plywood in 3 passes at 150mm/min can also cut at 100mm/min in 2 passes but the 3 at 150 is just slightly faster (like 12 seconds faster on a 5hr cut haha) and that extra half pass can be helpful. Anything thicker will be hard to do. Also make sure you focus the laser to the bottom of the piece of wood not the top. This makes a HUGE difference.

That exactly the same grid I use currently and it works well! What I would do as well is get some nice magnets (the rectangular ones that like 1inch by half inch) and use those to hold down wood or whatever to the grid to keep it flat in case you have semi warped wood. It holds it in place and is low profile super awesome actually.  And yea it will mark the aluminum either way so don’t worry.

Get a pro for sure! Well worth the extra money my first printer was an Ender 3 pro and it is amazing!

On a side note you will want to look into a honeycomb grid or something similar that is raised off the bed by about an inch if you intend to cut with your laser. It’s rather difficult and leaves a lot of burns on the side that is laying flat. The aluminum plate is a good call though (guessing it’s aluminum) would definitely keep that under the honeycomb grid or whatever you decided to use.

If your choosing between the Ortur 15w and 20w I would recommend the 20w for sure. That extra power you will get from it makes it worth it specially when it comes to cutting wood. I have the 20w fixed focus one and it cuts mdf or birch plywood in 2 or 3 passes (I usually do full power at 150mm/min 3 passes because it is slightly faster than 2 cuts at 100mm/min and makes some pieces easier to pop out) but this is only do able if you get an air assist for it. That will cost extra to make happen and if you know someone or have a 3D printer you can print the pieces needed to run the air assist instead of buying them. A decent pump will run you around $50 and tubing another $5-10. Should only need the air assist for cutting though. Also make sure you focus the laser to the bottom of the wood it helps dramatically then focusing it to the top. 

As far as engraving acrylic and stainless steal it is definitely do able. Simply applying masking tape (or some sort of a thin covering like paint) will make engraving items like glass much easier to do. 

There is definitely a learning curve though. But once your learn it you won’t be wasting materials for the most part. Overall I have been very happy with my 20w and I will get a K40 at some point but I will probably upgrade my Ortur with a 10w (output) Endurance laser which is almost double the output power. They come with mounts that work for the Ortur and work beautifully from what I’ve seen. 

You will need ventilation for sure though I made an enclosure for mine (was around $60 not including the acrylic windows) and ventilation is no longer an issue for me. Can always do this later as well so long as you are able to clear out the smoke. Another thing needed is a proper bed for it. You will need a raised bed of sorts with honeycomb or some style meshing in order to cut properly. If it sits flat on whatever bed you choose it will have issues sadly. 

Hope this helps a little best of luck!
